verdicts.rewritten_summary: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Malta with the compliance breakdown across asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime/hate speech and equality-body categories, scored per category on the map's red-to-green scale.

Legal status: same-sex conduct legal since 29 January 1973; civil unions since 2014 and same-sex marriage since 2017; gender change without surgery; full adoption since 2014; open military service; discrimination protections cover sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Academic chapter (Routledge Companion to Gender and Crime, 2025, Mary Grace Vella): Malta records one of the lowest SOGIE physical/sexual victimisation rates in the EU27, yet LGBTIQ+ people still report a higher share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

University of Malta dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024): four interviews with current/former transgender inmates at the Correctional Service Agency (25-year cohort) found healthcare, legislative and knowledge gaps plus post-release problems, with CSA practice out of sync with national gender-identity legislation — institutional lag beneath the strong statute book.

ICJ (30 July 2025): ICJ and partners filed observations in M.S. v. Malta at the ECtHR — an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in Malta in April 2023 received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024; submissions raise ECHR Articles 3/5/13 (non-refoulement, detention conditions, individualised assessment before detention). Direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at Maltese borders.

MaltaToday (15 April 2014): parliament approved the constitutional amendment naming gender identity — Malta the first European state to do so — and introduced civil unions in the same sitting; Transgender Europe was among the first NGOs to applaud gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

Outright International overview (updated March 2026): Section 377 used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence; after the 1 Feb 2021 coup risks intensified — torture/sexual violence in detention, Oct 2022 Organization Registration Law (prison terms for NGO non-compliance), compulsory military service announced Feb 2024, seven LGBTQ-themed books banned 2025. Verdict: avoid entirely.

DVB (Jan 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; the NUG recorded 17 LGBT killed and 2 critically injured since 1 Feb 2021; 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' found 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and 68%+ fear repercussions from abusers.

RFA (10 Jan 2025): junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; colonial-era law carries up to 10 years for gay sex; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the Feb 2021 coup.

ASEAN SOGIE Caucus (March 2025, from Queers of Burma Alternative research Jan 2025): the 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement; Section 377 carries life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and 1945 Police Act s.35(c) (face covering, up to 3 months) is used specifically against transgender people.

Guardian (2 Feb 2016): Colors Rainbow's work in Yangon — trans woman Nat Nat We describes arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work; documents routine police violence against trans women.

Washington Blade (2 Nov 2018): Aung Myo Htut (aka Addy Chen), an outspoken HIV-positive LGBTI advocate and Yangon restaurant owner, was charged under Penal Code 377 over an alleged offence against an employee — Section 377 in active use, with the community demanding fair media coverage.

HuffPost (17 Oct 2015): colonial-era criminalisation; 2013 Mandalay arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); nat kadaws (spirit mediums) are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.

Human Dignity Trust global legal history (updated 18 June 2026): Montenegro appears among the 1977 European decriminalisations (Croatia/Slovenia/Montenegro cohort); reference source for MNE's decriminalisation date rather than MNE-specific analysis.

GlobalGayz (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; small gay scene with deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, discrimination and harassment when visible; the first Podgorica Pride was cancelled in May 2011 after two attacks on gay people in the capital. Dated but concrete on social climate.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Pride marched through Podgorica — roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas; Queer Montenegro's Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible.' Shows both state protection and organised hostility.

PinkNews (2 Aug 2019): MPs blocked the same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing — ERA's Western Balkans office: LGBT people 'forced to live as second-class citizens' (no hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights); a 2018 ERA study found 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted.

CDM (Dec 2018): the Government adopted the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership granting couples near marriage-equivalent rights via registrar ceremony — explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; shows the reform trajectory before the 2019 parliamentary block.

Outright International (last updated 12 March 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised 1993; sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination prohibited but protections fragmented (no comprehensive law); marriage equality constitutionally prohibited with no union recognition; groups can register.
thin: no usable finding
verdicts.note: landing page only: regional report body not in fetch

verdicts.rewritten_summary: The Establishment (Aug 2018): profiles Anaraa Nyamdorj, trans man and co-founder/advisor of the LGBT Centre — came out in 2004, began transition in 2011; describes Mongolia's 2018 Pride and LGBT Centre advocacy; ground on trans life, transition access and acceptance in Ulaanbaatar.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2019): after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman, the LGBT Center trained police on the 2017 criminal code's hate-crime provisions — 500+ police officers, prosecutors and judges trained; force now has guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of ID documents.

GlobalGayz Mongolia report: no laws specifically against homosexuality though 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' provisions remain; the scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism; a 2008 account describes two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees fear being outed.

verdicts.note: rule-1/rule-5: generic parent-nation airport guide, MNP never the subject (consistent with ASM ruling)
rule-1: about Kansas birth-certificate policy, not MNP

verdicts.rewritten_summary: MAP Equality Profile: Northern Mariana Islands (data as of 27 Sep 2026): Sexual Orientation Policy Score 3.5/22 (Low), Gender Identity Policy Score -2/25 (Negative), overall 1.5/47 (Low); marriage recognition 1/1 since 2015, no comprehensive state nondiscrimination coverage beyond federal EEOC recourse — the scorecard a visitor faces.

adds.title: LGBT rights in the Northern Mariana Islands (Wikipedia)
adds.summary: Wikipedia overview: same-sex marriage legal since 2015 — first same-sex marriage on Saipan officiated 27 July 2015 (per Marianas Variety citation); adoption since 2015; gender changes legal provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process; discrimination protections limited to government employees beyond federal law. Backs up the blocked wikiwand mirror with canonical content.

adds.title: LGBT celebrates Gay Pride at GIG (Saipan Tribune)
adds.summary: Saipan Tribune: the CNMI's first-ever Gay Pride event was held at the GIG Discotheque in Garapan with about 60 people attending; organiser Sharmaine Casquero called it a success — on-the-ground evidence of visible, peaceful LGBT community life in the territory.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Outright International (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct legal since the 2015 penal code; no legal gender recognition procedure exists; societal attitudes broadly neutral but LGBTIQ people face family ostracisation and employment/education barriers; the 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations then disappointed. Freshness confirmed: the new 2024 penal code removed the employment non-discrimination protection that had existed.
verdicts.note: freshness: 2024 penal code removed employment non-discrimination protection (supersedes older claim text)

verdicts.rewritten_summary: GlobalGayz archive (2006-2011): dated milestones — first newspaper article arguing gay rights (Agencia de Informacao, 7 July 2006), Maputo men petitioning parliament, the LGBT group still unregistered as of March 2011, refugee deaths en route to South Africa; documents early organising under the colonial-era law.
Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2016) from Afrobarometer: Mozambique among Africa's more tolerant — 56% would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour (vs Uganda/Burkina Faso/Niger at 5%).

Global Voices (28 Nov 2017): after a decade of blocked applications (since 2008), the Constitutional Council — supreme court equivalent — ruled Lambda Mozambique's status did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration of the country's only LGBT organisation.

Guardian (30 June 2015): Mozambique's new penal code erased the colonial 'vices against nature' provision; Lambda (not yet officially registered at the time) pivoted to anti-discrimination lobbying; Lambda's Carina Capitine: the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries but does face discrimination.

Cairo 52 country review: transgender people effectively criminalised through 'debauchery' provisions — Penal Code Art. 264 carries 1 month to 2 years' jail and 5,000-150,000 ouguiya fines for public indecency/debauchery offences applied to gender nonconformity; grave lack of official data on the trans community.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report (Mauritania): consensual same-sex conduct criminalised but penalties not enforced; reports of violence and threats against LGBT people; civil society objected to scant indictments and officials sometimes acted with impunity.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Jan 2026, from Outright): the Penal Code keeps a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men; the government confirmed a de facto death-penalty moratorium in 2021; arrests and detentions under the provisions continue in recent years; low visibility drives stigma; since 2008 the country has served as refuge for Senegulese LGBTIQ people.

Liberals Mauritania (organisation website, c)2026): openly campaigns from within Mauritania on freethinker and LGBT-adjacent causes — titles include 'When the Law Deprives Rights and Freedoms' and 'The First Trans Woman to Speak Out in Mauritania's Media' — evidence of a minimal but real public advocacy space.

GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption that wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north; gay life barely exists locally ('gays are everywhere but hardly here') — decimated social scene; dated but concrete.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.
